{"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"Product Strategy","url":"https://app.notion.com/p/31167c87082c81d6bb45ce8ce133056d?pvs=204","text":"Here is the result of "fetch" for the Page with URL https://app.notion.com/p/31167c87082c81d6bb45ce8ce133056d as of 2026-02-27T00:40:42.654Z: {"title":"Product Strategy"} ## 2026-02-24 — Initial Vision: The Agent Economy ### Vision Build the economic infrastructure for autonomous agents — starting with a marketplace where agents deliver outcomes for businesses, evolving into the trust layer and commerce network that powers the entire agent economy. ### The Thesis We are at the beginning of a fundamental shift in how work gets done. AI agents can now connect to any system via MCP, reason across multiple data sources, and take actions — not just analyze. This means any workflow that today requires a human to synthesize information from multiple sources and produce structured output is now automatable. But the real transformation isn't "agents help humans work faster." That's where everyone is focused today. The real transformation is **agents transacting with other agents on behalf of their principals.** When Agent A can discover, negotiate with, and pay Agent B to get work done — without humans in the loop for routine tasks — you get an entirely new form of economic activity. That world needs infrastructure that doesn't exist yet: a marketplace for agent-delivered outcomes, a trust and identity layer for verifying agents, and a commerce protocol for agent-to-agent transactions. We will build all three — in sequence. ### Why Now Three things converged in 2025: 1. **MCP became the universal standard.** Anthropic's Model Context Protocol was donated to the Linux Foundation and adopted by OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Salesforce, and NVIDIA. 5,800+ MCP servers, 300+ clients. Agents can programmatically connect to virtually any data source or service. 2. **Agent quality crossed the threshold.** LLMs can now produce institutional-quality analysis, writing, and reasoning. The output is good enough that businesses will pay for it as a replacement for expensive human labor. 3. **The infrastructure layer got funded.** Companies like Smithery, Manufact (\$6.3M), Runlayer (\$11M), and Alpic (€5.1M) are building MCP hosting, security, deployment. The foundation is being poured. What's missing is the economic layer on top. ### Current Focus Defining the Phase 1 MVP — the Delegation Economy. Specifically: choosing the first vertical, scoping the product, and identifying the first customers. ### Key Bets 1. **Outcomes over tasks.** Companies will pay for delivered outcomes ("competitive landscape report") rather than hiring humans or configuring AI tools themselves. 2. **Agent operators are a new economic actor.** Entrepreneurs who build, train, and run specialized agents can earn income from agent output — a new category between freelancing and SaaS. 3. **Three-phase sequencing works.** Starting with human-in-the-loop marketplace (Phase 1) generates the data needed for trust infrastructure (Phase 2), which enables fully autonomous agent commerce (Phase 3). 4. **Trust is the bottleneck.** The agent economy can't scale without verifiable agent identity and reputation. Whoever builds this infrastructure owns a critical chokepoint. 5. **We can bootstrap supply.** By being the first agent operator ourselves, we avoid the cold start problem that kills most marketplaces. ### Not Doing - Not building AI infrastructure (MCP hosting, security, deployment) — that layer is being funded and built by others - Not building AI tools or copilots — we're building the economy where agents transact, not making humans faster - Not competing with freelance marketplaces (Upwork, Fiverr) — we guarantee outcomes, not connect buyers to humans - Not starting with fully autonomous agent-to-agent commerce — building trust infrastructure first ### Three-Phase Strategy **Phase 1 — The Delegation Economy (Build 3)** A marketplace where companies post desired outcomes and agent operators bid to deliver them. Humans define outcomes. Agents deliver them. We are the first agent operator, bootstrapping supply while building the platform. Key design principles: Buyers think in business outcomes (never technology). Agent operators are entrepreneurs (not developers). Transparency without micromanagement. Quality is the moat. MVP vertical: Market research and competitive intelligence. Perfect because outcomes are clearly definable, quality is verifiable, immediately valuable to any B2B company, and we can build agents to do this work ourselves. **Phase 2 — Agent Identity & Reputation Layer (Build 2)** Verifiable reputation and identity system for AI agents — credit bureau meets SSL certificates meets Yelp reviews. Built on real transaction data from Phase 1. Exposed as open API/protocol for any platform to integrate. Strategic goal: become the Visa network of agent trust. **Phase 3 — Agent-to-Agent Commerce Network (Build 1)** Full vision: protocol and network where agents discover, negotiate with, and transact with other agents on behalf of their principals. Phase 1 with the human removed from routine transactions. Requires trust infrastructure from Phase 2. ### The Flywheel Phase 1 generates transaction data → feeds Phase 2 reputation scores → enables trust for Phase 3 autonomous transactions → generates more transaction data → strengthens reputation scores → enables more autonomous transactions. ### Market Context - AI agents market: \$7-8B (2025) → \$50B+ (2030), \~45% CAGR - MCP ecosystem: \$1.2B → \$4.5B in 2025 alone - 5,800+ MCP servers, 300+ clients - Infrastructure companies funded: Smithery, Manufact (\$6.3M), Runlayer (\$11M), Alpic (€5.1M) - No marketplace for agent-delivered outcomes exists yet - No reputation or identity standard for agents exists yet - No protocol for agent-to-agent commercial transactions exists yet ### Competitive Positioning We are NOT: a consulting firm, an AI tool/copilot, an infrastructure provider, a freelance marketplace. We ARE: the economic layer of the agent ecosystem — a marketplace, trust infrastructure, and commerce protocol. --- ## Change Log ## 2026-02-27 — Composable Architecture: Build in Spinnable Units, Ride the Giants ### What Changed Market research into agent identity revealed that Visa (Trusted Agent Protocol), Ping Identity, WSO2, OpenID Foundation, Incode, Prove, and Vouched are all building agent authentication and authorization infrastructure. This is layer 1 — "is this agent who it claims to be?" and "is this agent allowed to do X?" Nobody is building layer 2 — "is this agent *good* at what it claims?" — because nobody has the transaction data. That layer requires real outcomes with quality ratings, delivery history, and capability verification built from actual work. Strale's capability marketplace generates exactly this data. ### Strategic Principle: Composable Units Strale builds products as architecturally independent units that work together but could each stand alone. Each unit should: - Have its own API surface (separate from other units) - Store its own data (not entangled with other units' schemas) - Have a clear standalone value proposition - Be spinnable into a separate product/company if it gains independent traction This is not a plan to split the company. It's an architecture decision that preserves optionality and forces clean boundaries. ### The Units **Unit 1 — Capability Marketplace (current build)** What it is: SDK + API + wallet for developers to discover and call 200+ capabilities. Standalone value: Developer tool. Competes with RapidAPI model but for the agent era. Revenue: Per-call pricing, subscriptions. Data it generates: Usage patterns, demand signals, capability reliability metrics. **Unit 2 — Agent Reputation Engine (build next)** What it is: API that scores agent/capability quality based on real transaction outcomes. Standalone value: Any platform can query "how reliable is this agent?" before transacting. Revenue: API calls for reputation queries, premium analytics. Data it needs: Transaction history from Unit 1 (and eventually from external platforms). Depends on: Unit 1 generating enough transaction volume to make scores meaningful. **Unit 3 — Commerce Protocol (build last)** What it is: The discover → negotiate → transact → verify → rate protocol for agent-to-agent commerce. Standalone value: The Visa network of agent commerce. Revenue: Transaction fees on agent-to-agent trades. Data it needs: Reputation scores from Unit 2 to enable trust between unknown agents. Depends on: Unit 2 having credible reputation data, and the market being ready (2028-2030). ### Relationship to Giants **Don't compete. Compose.** - Visa/Mastercard are building *payment identity* for agents (can this agent spend money?). We build *capability reputation* on top of their payment rails. - Ping Identity/WSO2/Okta are building *access control* for agents (is this agent authorized?). We build *quality scoring* that their customers query after auth. - OpenID Foundation is defining *identity standards*. We implement those standards and add the reputation data layer they can't build. - MCP/A2A protocols handle *communication*. We handle *economic trust* — the layer that says "this agent is worth hiring." The giants build authentication (is it real?). We build reputation (is it good?). Authentication is table stakes. Reputation is the moat. ### Timeline - **Now → Month 3:** Unit 1 generates transaction data. Architect Unit 2's data model but don't expose it yet. - **Month 3-6:** Unit 2 API goes live. Internal reputation scores visible on capabilities. Begin collecting structured quality feedback. - **Month 6-12:** Unit 2 opens to external queries. Other platforms can check capability/agent reputation via API. This is the moment it could become independently valuable. - **Month 12+:** Evaluate whether Unit 2 has more traction as an independent product than as part of Strale. If external query volume exceeds internal usage, consider spinning it out. ### Key Bets (Updated) Previous bets still hold. Adding: 1. **Composable architecture creates optionality.** Building in independent units means we can respond to market signals — if one unit breaks out, we can double down or spin out. If one unit fails, others survive. 2. **Reputation requires transaction data.** The giants can't build credible agent reputation because they don't run a marketplace. Our marketplace is the unfair advantage for the reputation layer. 3. **Ride, don't fight.** Every standard the giants ship (Visa TAP, OpenID agent identity, MCP auth) makes our reputation layer more valuable, not less. We build on their work. ### Not Doing (Updated) - Not building agent authentication (Visa, Ping Identity, OpenID are handling this) - Not building agent access control (IAM vendors own this) - Not building bot detection (Vouched, Cloudflare own this) - Not proposing competing identity standards (adopt whatever wins) - Not racing to ship Unit 3 before the market is ready (2028-2030 at earliest) ## 2026-02-27 — Scaling via Protocol Integration: Piggybacking on the Giants ### The Insight Four open protocols are being built by trillion-dollar companies right now. Together they solve communication, payment identity, and access control for agents. But they all explicitly leave one problem unsolved: **quality reputation and capability-based discovery.** The A2A spec literally punts this to implementers. That gap is Strale Unit 2. Instead of building competing infrastructure, Strale becomes a **node in every network the giants are building**, then fills the gap they deliberately left open. ### The Four Protocols and What They Give Strale for Free **1. MCP (Anthropic → Linux Foundation) — Agent-to-tool communication** Strale is already an MCP server. Every MCP client (Claude, Cursor, Windsurf, 300+ clients) can discover and call Strale capabilities as tools. This is the current distribution channel. What it gives us: Tool-level integration with every major AI assistant. **2. A2A (Google → Linux Foundation, v0.3, 150+ organizations) — Agent-to-agent communication** Open protocol for agents to discover each other, exchange tasks, and collaborate. Every A2A agent publishes an "Agent Card" at `/.well-known/agent-card.json` — a JSON file listing identity, skills, auth requirements, and endpoint. Google, Microsoft, SAP, Salesforce, ServiceNow, Adobe, Box, UiPath all building A2A support. What it gives us: Automatic discovery by the entire A2A ecosystem without marketing effort. **Critical detail:** A2A explicitly leaves discovery infrastructure, registries, and reputation to implementers. The spec says this is "up to you." [Solo.io](http://Solo.io) has written about this gap — calling out the need for Agent Registries, Agent Naming Services, and capability-based discovery. **This is literally Unit 2.** The protocol was designed with a slot shaped exactly like what we're building. **3. Visa TAP (open on GitHub, RFC 9421) — Cryptographic agent payment identity** Agents sign HTTP requests with private keys. Merchants verify via Visa's public keys. Partners include Stripe, Shopify, Adyen, Cloudflare, Akamai. Already completing hundreds of live agent-initiated transactions. What it gives us: Payment infrastructure we don't need to build. Any Visa-authenticated agent can purchase Strale capabilities. **4. OpenID / IAM Standards — Agent identity and access management** Ping Identity, Auth0/Okta, WSO2 all shipping agent IAM. OpenID Foundation published a whitepaper (Oct 2025) defining the problem. Standards still forming but converging on token exchange and delegated authorization. What it gives us: Enterprise auth infrastructure. We implement their standards, not our own. ### What Nobody Is Building: Layer 5
Layer Problem Who's building it Strale's role
Communication How do agents talk? Google (A2A), Anthropic (MCP) Implement both
Payment identity Can this agent pay? Visa (TAP), Mastercard Accept their credentials
Access control Is this agent authorized? Ping Identity, WSO2, Okta Use their standards
Bot detection Agent or malicious bot? Vouched, Cloudflare, Akamai Not our problem
**Quality reputation** **Is this agent good?** **Nobody** **This is Unit 2**
A2A Agent Cards describe what an agent *claims* it can do. Visa TAP verifies the agent *is who it claims to be*. IAM verifies the agent *is authorized to act*. But nobody verifies the agent *is actually good at what it claims*. That requires real transaction data from a marketplace. The giants can't build this because they don't run one. ### The Scaling Phases **Phase A — Become discoverable on every protocol (Now → Month 3)** Strale already speaks MCP. Add A2A Agent Cards for all 200+ capabilities. This is not a big build — it's publishing JSON files at a well-known endpoint. Each capability becomes a discoverable A2A agent with skills, endpoint, and auth method. Distribution shift: From "developers find us via Product Hunt" to "agents find us via protocol discovery." Any of the 150+ organizations building A2A clients can now find and use Strale capabilities automatically. **Phase B — Become the registry that annotates Agent Cards with reputation (Month 3-6)** A2A has Agent Cards but no reputation. The spec explicitly punts on this. Strale builds the missing piece: a registry that indexes Agent Cards from across the ecosystem and annotates them with quality scores, reliability metrics, and transaction history. Any A2A client can query Strale's registry to find not just which agents exist, but which agents are good. **This is like Google indexing the web. A2A Agent Cards are web pages. Strale's registry is the search engine that ranks them.** This is Unit 2 becoming real — and it scales with A2A adoption, not with Strale's marketing budget. **Phase C — Accept protocol-native payments (Month 6-12)** Accept Visa TAP for agent-initiated purchases. An agent with Visa TAP credentials can discover Strale via A2A, verify capability reputation via the registry, and purchase with cryptographically signed payment. No custom auth, no Strale-specific wallet. Just protocol-standard commerce. This means any agent in Visa's Intelligent Commerce ecosystem (100+ partners) can buy Strale capabilities without any Strale-specific integration. ### The Compound Effect Without protocol integration: Strale grows linearly with marketing effort. Each new user requires discovery, signup, SDK integration. With protocol integration: Strale grows with the adoption curves of MCP, A2A, and Visa TAP — all of which have billion-dollar companies spending billions to drive adoption. Every new A2A client is a potential Strale customer who discovers us automatically. Every new Visa TAP agent is a potential buyer who can pay without onboarding. **We don't compete with these networks. We're a node in all of them. The more they grow, the more agents discover and use Strale.** ### Implications for Unit Architecture This sharpens the composable units: **Unit 1 (Capability Marketplace)** exposes capabilities as both MCP tools and A2A agents. Accepts both Strale wallet and Visa TAP payments. Generates transaction data. **Unit 2 (Agent Reputation Registry)** indexes A2A Agent Cards across the entire ecosystem — not just Strale capabilities. Annotates with quality scores from Unit 1 transaction data, plus reliability metrics from monitoring any A2A endpoint. This is the unit most likely to become independently massive, because it serves the entire A2A ecosystem, not just Strale users. **Unit 3 (Commerce Protocol)** becomes unnecessary as a separate build if A2A + Visa TAP + Supertab mature. The giants may build the commerce rails themselves. Strale's value shifts from "we built the protocol" to "we're the reputation layer every protocol participant queries before transacting." This is actually a stronger position — protocol-agnostic trust infrastructure. ### Key Bets (Updated) 1. **A2A adoption is the rising tide.** 150+ organizations and the Linux Foundation ensure A2A becomes a standard. Strale rides that wave. 2. **The reputation gap in A2A is structural, not accidental.** The spec intentionally delegates discovery/reputation to implementers. This is an invitation, not an oversight. 3. **Unit 3 may not need to be built.** If A2A + payment protocols mature, the commerce rails exist. Strale's endgame may be the reputation layer, not the commerce protocol. This is a stronger position anyway — protocol-agnostic infrastructure vs. yet another protocol. ### Risks - A2A adoption could stall or fragment (mitigated by Linux Foundation governance and 150+ backers) - Google could build the registry/reputation layer into A2A itself (mitigated by their pattern of leaving application layers to the ecosystem — Google built HTTP, not Yelp) - Visa TAP could remain consumer-focused and not extend to B2B agent commerce (mitigated by Supertab and Ramp already doing B2B on these rails)
